newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs in Croatia complete 'free and fair' vote.
newsitem.headline: Serbs in Croatia complete 'free and fair' vote.

text.p: Former rebel Serbs have completed their first election in post-independence Croatia, judged by the United Nations to be fair despite technical hitches that almost ruined it.

Voting in Eastern Slavonia, which reverts to Croatian rule this summer after a period under U.N. protection, coincided with Sunday's regional elections across Croatia, but was extended into Monday to make up time for technical delays.
The ruling nationalist Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) cruised to a landslide win in 17 of 21 county assemblies.
It lost only two, while there were stalemates between the HDZ and the opposition in two counties previously run by the HDZ, according to a final unofficial count announced on Monday.
Organisational bungling that led to misplaced and insufficient ballot forms halted voting in Eastern Slavonia for hours on Sunday.

The U.N. blamed the delay on poor planning by Croatian electoral authorities supplying voting materials. Zagreb officials put it down to uncertainty over the number of Serb voters, who were still registering as late as Saturday night.
Franc Vasallo, U.N. election coordinator in Eastern Slavonia, said there was still no way to estimate how many people had actually voted. Roughly 150,000 were eligible.
U.N. mission spokesman Philip Arnold said the first unofficial results would be released on Tuesday.

"On behalf of (U.N. administrator Jacques) Klein, I can say that he is confident the election will be certified as fair and free," Arnold told a news conference in Vukovar, Eastern Slavonia's largest town, still in ruins from a 1991 war.

Klein, a U.S. diplomat in charge of the mission, has 30 days to formally certify the voting in which a single Serb party bloc was pitted against the HDZ backed by Croatian refugees who are keen to reclaim their property.
Eastern Slavonia is the one remaining enclave seized by minority Serbs in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia. Two others were recaptured in war in 1995.
In the capital Zagreb, a centre-left opposition coalition appeared to have edged ahead of the HDZ in a popular vote for the city assembly.
The Social Democrats (SDP) - former communists - finished with 24.18 percent and Social Liberals (HSLS) 12.58 percent for a combined 36.76 percent of the vote, while the HDZ gained 35.67 percent.

The reversal did not mean the opposition would take over the powerful Zagreb regional government, since the HDZ again re-emerged as the biggest single vote getter and its rivals fell well short of a viable majority.

Tudjman's party wasted no time beginning post-electoral manoeuvring by offering "cooperation" to the HSLS and Croatian Peasant Party, which won eight percent, in a bid to achieve a one-seat majority in the assembly.
The HDZ overture was aimed at splintering the opposition coalition. HSLS leaders have mulled "cooperation" with the HDZ in the past but the party is divided over the issue.

The HDZ lost to a loose seven-party coalition in Zagreb in 1995 but Tudjman, citing "national security" as grounds, vetoed four opposition mayoral nominees and imposed a provisional HDZ city administration.

His move brought accusations of authoritarianism and was condemned in the West. Tudjman argued the HDZ had won a "relative majority" while the opposition was an unstable mishmash of parties ranging from far left to far right.

HDZ Zagreb party chairman Zlatko Canjuga claimed the party had posted "a complete and clear" victory on Sunday because its rivals were not a genuine coalition, a view mirroring Tudjman's belief that no other Croatian party or bloc is fit to govern.
Even if the opposition took power in the capital this time, they would face obstruction by the HDZ-dominated county council which holds key financial and political levers in the region.

To have any chance of gaining power, the SDP and HSLS would have to lure the HSS to its cause. But the Peasant Party has rejected alliances with the SDP because of its communist past in pre-1991 federal Yugoslavia.

The HDZ, which flaunted Tudjman's "Father-of-the-Nation" charisma in the campaign, won 41 of 63 seats in parliament's upper House of Counties. Opposition parties took 22, of which two are reserved for Serbs from Eastern Slavonia.
